catalog_quote: Une phrase interrogative semble avoir surtout deux intona- tions, d'après que la phrase ordinaire a des tons hauts ou non . S'il y a des tons hauts, les intervalles sont plus grands: (- nurukoba rwaanjye ? est - ce ma peau ? -), et les tons préparatoires sont plus marqués, au détriment du ton haut même: agatsíma karasígaye, il reste un peu de pâte ... S'il y avait un accent d'intensité caractérisant l'un ou l'autre élément, on s'attendrait à une prononciation différente de paires de mots comme la suivante: ba - ra - ru - tan - a ils l'étirent (la peau) ba - ra - rut - an - a ils se surpassent l'un l'autre Or on dit indifféremment dans les deux cas: bararutana . MORPHOLOGIE La morphologie comprendra, après une introduction morphonologique, [running header:] 20 ESSAI DE GRAMMAIRE RUNDI.

sweep_summary: Rundi (rund1242) is not in the catalog. The two title-hit items could not be read: Philippson's 1991/92 Paris 5 thèse d'État 'Tons et accent dans les langues bantu d'Afrique orientale' (542 pp., Rundi among 47 languages) exists only in print/ANRT reproduction (theses.fr 'accessible: non'; not on HAL, archive.org, DDL or LLACAN pages) — its abstract frames East Bantu prosody as a scale from fully tonal to penultimate demarcative stress, but says nothing Rundi-specific; priority high as the best comparative accent source. Its published summary (Philippson 1998, Faits de langues 11-12: 429-440, Persée) was found but the PDF is bot-blocked (not reachable by automated download). Rodegem 1962 'Vocabulaire accentué' (ronéotypé, 90 pp.) is a tone-marked wordlist with no trace anywhere online (SUDOC 0, archive.org 0; priority low. Best first-hand statement read: Stevick 1965 FSI Kirundi Basic Course pp. 12-15 — two tones LOW/HIGH, mora-based placement, no stress anywhere in the book; Ménard 1908 §§53-62/474-482 gives placement rules for a lexical 'accent' that is high tone/length, and Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989 p. 40 report one High per phonological word in non-focus verbs ('more like an accentual language'). No source read states a word-stress rule for Rundi; it should be recorded as a tone language (no stress record), with Meeussen 1959 / Rodegem 1967 / Philippson 1991 as the print sources still to be checked. was already exhausted (2000/2000) before this search of works with stress in the title; all look-ups were direct downloads and catalog APIs. new_statements.quote: In Kirundi however, as in most African languages, pitch has functions which it does not have in English. [...] Pitch, then, may be the only audible difference between two words of entirely different meanings. To say the same thing in technical terms, Kirundi has LEXICALLY SIGNIFICANT distinctions of pitch. [p. 11] [...] In Kirundi, as in many other Bantu languages, the pitch phenomena are best described in terms of two tones, called LOW [and] HIGH. Low tone is quite simple: its typical realization is as a level, relatively low pitch [...] As its name implies, high tone ordinarily involves the use of a relatively high pitch, but this pitch is not level. [p. 13]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kirundi is described as a two-tone (High/Low) language in which pitch is lexically and grammatically distinctive and is counted on moras (short vowel = 1 mora, long = 2); the source describes tone placement per verb form and noun class and never invokes stress or intensity prominence. No source opened states a word-stress position, and none explicitly denies stress. Later analyses (Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989: 40; Jouannet 1989: 11-12) call the system 'accentual' in the pitch accent sense (at most one High per phonological word in non-focus verb forms), not stress.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any source opened.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. Tone: 'anticipated' high tone spills onto the preceding syllable; a 'provisional high tone' on /ni/, /si/ appears only after a non-pause (Stevick 1965: 21). Ménard 1908 (pp. 19-25, 282-286) gives lexical placement rules for his 'accent', which is high tone/length, not stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level tone described on citation forms and in sentence frames (FSI dialogues); Stevick notes utterance-final vs non-final differences in tone realization (e.g. twaakubuuye forms, p. 11).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe standard Kirundi of Burundi (rund1242; ISO run). The FSI course was prepared with Barundi speakers who lack the j/jy, c/cy, sh/shy contrasts 'present in some dialects' (Stevick 1965: xlvi); Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989 use Sabimana's own judgments. Ménard 1908 is the same language a century earlier (missionary orthography).

new_statements.quote: In Kirundi, as in many other Bantu languages, the pitch phenomena are best described in terms of two tones, called LOW [and] HIGH. Low tone is quite simple: its typical realization is as a level, relatively low pitch [...] As its name implies, high tone ordinarily involves the use of a relatively high pitch, but this pitch is not level. It most commonly consists of a rise followed immediately by a fall [...] A MORA is a unit of vowel length. Vowels in Kirundi may consist of either one or two moras, and no more. [...] The high tone may be attached to a vowel (whether long or short) at either of two PITCH POINTS. [...] There is never more than one high tone per mora
new_statements.citation: Stevick, Earl W. (with Raymond Setukura et al.) 1965. Kirundi Basic Course. Washington DC: Foreign Service Institute, US Department of State. catalog record, Note 1 'The use of the terms pitch and tone', pp. 12-15.
new_statements.locator: catalog record, Note 1, pp. 12-13 (scan pp. 12-13 of the 589-page PDF)
new_statements.reading: Kirundi word prosody is a two-tone (H/L) system with mora-sensitive placement of H; the book (589 pp.) never mentions stress. This is the clearest first-hand, English-language description read in this search of works with stress in the title. Two refinements read alongside it: Ménard 1908 §§53-62 (pp. 19-24) and §§474-482 (pp. 282-285) give placement rules for a lexically distributed 'accent' (grave mark, 'équivaut à peu près à notre accent circonflexe'; monosyllabic radicals and final syllables never take it, radical-initial vowels and vowels before NC usually do) which is the pre-tonological rendering of high tone/length, not stress; Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989 (Modèles en tonologie, p. 40) note that in non-focus verb forms 'there can be only one High tone per phonological word', so these forms 'look more like an accentual language than a tone language', and (p. 20) that tone-shift rules are sensitive to odd/even mora counts, 'found to date only in metrical stress systems'. Net: no source read states a word-stress position for Rundi; it is coded in the literature as a tone language with a culminative (one-H-per-word) accentual tendency in part of the verb system.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog: no-word-stress (Meeussen 1959 pp.18-19: no 'accent d'intensité'; WALS/Stevick: two-tone H/L system). Philippson, working largely from Meeussen 1959, Coupez 1980, Jouannet 1985 and Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989, codes Rwanda/Rundi as 'langue tonale', not accentual, with a penultimate unmarked for pitch, length or intensity: same type (tonal, no stress). It refines the existing statement's note on Goldsmith & Sabimana by explicitly rejecting their metrical/accentual reading of Kirundi H-repetition, and adds the mora-based tonal rule set (anticipation, Meeussen's rule, final-H retraction onto a long penult).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Philippson classifies Rwanda-Rundi (his group II, Western Highlands) as a tone language ('langue tonale'), explicitly NOT an accent language by his definition, because disyllabic noun stems show three underlying tonal patterns (-cvcv) and long-vowel stems five (-cv:cv), so L tones cannot be supplied by default. Word prosody = H/L tones on moras with Meeussen's rule (systematic), general association convention, lexical retraction of a stem-final H onto a long all-L penult (except pattern 5), H-repetition on the initial mora of each element prefixed to an H-bearing stem, displacement of a word-initial H to the next mora, and post-lexical anticipation of every H onto the preceding mora ('anticipation tonale'). On prominence: in the typology of the penultimate (ch.6 §3.5.2) rwanda-rundi is placed in class (d), languages whose penultimate is NOT marked by a culmination of pitch, length or intensity but only serves as a limit for tonal associations (final H, also on the penult by regressive association, dissociates before absolute pause; final H retracted onto the second mora of a long L penult); the annexe's rubric 10 'statut de la syllabe pénultième' for Rwanda/Rundi is just 'cf. 9' (tonal rules), in contrast with Nyoro/Tooro 'accent démarcatif (culmination de hauteur)' or Nande 'culmination d'intensité et de longueur'. Diachronically Rundi is at his 'stade II' (HH/HB neutralised via regressive dissimilation) and 'in transition towards an accentual system' (pp.199-200), and he rejects the binary-metrical analysis of Kirundi H-repetition proposed by Jouannet 1985 and Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989 as 'une illusion' due to monosyllabic pre-radical morphemes (p.198). Net: no word stress position is stated; the only stress-relevant statements are negative (tonal, not accentual; no penultimate prominence).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: no stress of any degree is posited; the only culminative-like facts are tonal (Meeussen's rule deleting the second of two adjacent H; Goldsmith & Sabimana's one-H-per-word/binary-metrical reading is discussed and rejected, pp.198-199).
new_statements.exceptions: Dialectal: 'rundi oriental' (after Meeussen) has merged -cvc&v with -c&vcv (um&ug&ozi), 'Hima' parlers keep umugoz&i > umug&oz&i but dissociate the final H before pause and before another H, rundi 'standard' dissociates it everywhere (table p.193); a few unexplained lexical exceptions to regressive association among monosyllabic H noun stems (um&uti 'arbre', p.191 n.1); pattern (e) mahweer&a is rare/marginal; Shubi and Hangaza (historically Rundi dialects in Tanzania) share the Rwanda-Rundi tonal system (p.412). By contrast Nyoro, Tooro and some Nyankore/Kiga sub-dialects (group III, not Rundi) have lost distinctive prosody and have a demarcative penultimate accent (p.412, 499).
new_statements.identity_note: Philippson treats 'rwanda-rundi' jointly (his group II, Hautes Terres de l'Ouest; Rundi = JD62), with Rundi-specific subsections (ch.4 §5.2.3-5.2.4) distinguishing rundi 'standard', 'rundi oriental' and 'Hima' parlers (after Meeussen 1959) and noting that Shubi and Hangaza share the system; his Rundi sources (bibliography pp.516-517) are second-hand: Goldsmith & Sabimana 1989, Meeussen 1959, Stevick et al. 1965 (Rwanda: Coupez 1980, Furere & Rialland 1983, Jouannet 1985/1989, Kimenyi 1976/1988, Sibomana 1974). Rodegem 1962 concerns Kirundi as recorded at the White Fathers' language centre (Ngozi), variety unspecified.

Bujumbura: Université du Burundi, Faculté des Lettres et Sciences Humaines, Département de Langues et Cultures Africaines. 55 pp.
tone_statements.quote: Le kirundi fait typologiquement partie des langues à système tonal privatif /H/ vs /Ø/, c’est-à-dire des langues où un ton (H)aut ne contraste pas avec un ton (B)as dans une opposition binaire, mais où il s’oppose à une absence de ton dans une opposition qui est donc privative (Rialland, 1998). Dans sa représentation phonologique sous-jacente, le kirundi, comme les autres langues de la même typologie [...], possède un seul niveau de hauteur distinctif (le ton H) ; le ton bas est attribué par défaut aux syllabes atones au niveau de surface, i.e. le niveau phonétique (Hyman, 2000).
tone_statements.translation: Typologically, Kirundi belongs to the languages with a privative tone system /H/ vs /Ø/, i.e. languages in which a High tone does not contrast with a Low tone in a binary opposition but is opposed to the absence of tone, an opposition that is therefore privative (Rialland 1998). In its underlying phonological representation Kirundi, like the other languages of the same type [...], has a single distinctive pitch level (the H tone); low tone is assigned by default to toneless syllables at the surface, i.e. phonetic, level (Hyman 2000).

sources.quote: Ces systèmes varient en effet depuis des langues pleinement tonales (kikuyu) jusqu'à des langues à accent démarcatif pénultième (swahili), tous les cas intermédiaires étant représentés. [...] on propose l'hypothèse que le moteur principal de l'évolution des systèmes concernés a été l'émergence d'un accent démarcatif sur la pénultième servant de limite de domaine pour l'association tonale. (theses.fr abstract) — 'These systems range from fully tonal languages (Kikuyu) to languages with demarcative penultimate accent (Swahili), all intermediate cases being represented ... the main driver of the evolution of these systems was the emergence of a demarcative penultimate accent serving as a domain boundary for tone association.'
sources.note: Comparative typology of tone and accent across ~30-47 East Bantu languages (Glottolog lists Rundi [run] among the 47 covered). The abstract places languages on a scale from purely tonal to purely penultimate-stress; where Rundi sits on that scale is not stated in the abstract, and the Rundi section was not read. sources.note: §3 'De l'accent' §§53-62 pp. 19-25 and Supplément §§474-482 pp. 282-286: 'L'accent tonique ordinaire équivaut à peu près à notre accent circonflexe' (p. 20); place of the 'accent' is lexical and given by lists/rules (monosyllabic roots never take it; final syllables always short; disyllabic roots either unaccented or accented on the first syllable; vowel-initial roots, contracted vowels, vowels before prenasalised C, Cw syllables take it). This 'accent' (grave mark) is the pre-tonological rendering of high tone/length, not stress in the modern sense.

tone.translation: Typologically, Kirundi belongs to the languages with a privative tone system /H/ vs /Ø/, i.e. languages in which a High tone does not contrast with a Low tone in a binary opposition but is opposed to the absence of tone, an opposition that is therefore privative (Rialland 1998). In its underlying phonological representation Kirundi, like the other languages of the same type [...], has a single distinctive pitch level (the H tone); low tone is assigned by default to toneless syllables at the surface, i.e. phonetic, level (Hyman 2000).
